title: Bullet Trains
summary: In 1964 Japan opened a brand-new railway with sleek trains that zoomed along at 210 km/h, faster than any regular train before. People called them bullet trains. Soon France, Germany, Spain and China built their own super-fast trains, and engineers dug amazing tunnels under the sea and through the mountains.

sections.heading: A Crowded Country and a Bold Old Man
paragraphs: Picture Japan in the 1950s. The country was recovering from the terrible destruction of the Second World War, and its factories were growing fast. Most of its people and industry were squeezed into a narrow strip along the Pacific coast, between Tokyo and Osaka. The old railway joining them, the Tōkaidō Main Line, was one of the busiest in the world, and it was jammed. Trains crawled along tracks built to a narrow gauge of 1,067 mm (3 ft 6 in), which made them less stable at high speed than trains on wider track. The line could not carry many more passengers or much more freight.

Japan's railway planners had dreamed of something better before. In 1939 they had drawn up plans for a fast new line, and newspapers nicknamed the proposed trains dangan ressha, which means 'bullet train'. War stopped the project. But the name was never forgotten.

In 1955 a 71-year-old man named Shinji Sogō became president of Japanese National Railways, or JNR. Many people thought he was too old for the job, but Sogō was full of energy and determined to build a completely new railway. Instead of squeezing more trains onto the old narrow track, he wanted a separate, wider-gauge line built only for fast passenger trains. Many experts thought the idea was foolish. Airliners and motorways were the future, they said, and railways were finished.

Sogō needed a brilliant engineer, so he brought back Hideo Shima, who had designed steam locomotives for Japan's railways and had left JNR a few years earlier. Shima was born in Osaka in 1901 and had studied mechanical engineering at Tokyo Imperial University. Years before, he had suggested a radical idea: instead of one heavy locomotive pulling the whole train, put electric motors under many of the carriages. This 'distributed power' would spread the weight more evenly, reduce the pounding on the track and let the train accelerate and brake more smoothly. It became a key feature of the bullet train.

Building the new line was a gigantic job. Construction began on 20 April 1959. The route needed thousands of bridges and many tunnels, and it had to cope with a country shaken by frequent earthquakes. Japan asked the World Bank, an international lender, for help, and in the early 1960s received a loan of 80 million US dollars, much less than the railway had hoped for and only a small slice of the total cost. To persuade the government to support the project, Sogō is often said to have presented a lower cost estimate than he expected, knowing that once the work had begun, nobody would want to stop it halfway.

The costs did rise far above the original budget. In 1963, before the line even opened, both Sogō and Shima were forced to resign. Shima's career was far from over, though. In 1969 he became head of Japan's new space agency, NASDA, and helped develop its rockets.

sections.heading: 1 October 1964: The Future Arrives
paragraphs: Early on the morning of 1 October 1964, two gleaming trains set off at the same moment, one from Tokyo and one from Osaka. The Tōkaidō Shinkansen was open. The name Shinkansen simply means 'new trunk line' in Japanese, but the rest of the world soon called the trains bullet trains.

The timing was perfect. Nine days later, on 10 October, the Tokyo Olympic Games opened, the first Olympics ever held in Asia. Visitors from all over the world arrived to find a country that had rebuilt itself after the war, and a train that seemed to belong to the 21st century.

The first trains are known as the 0 Series. They were painted ivory white with a blue stripe, and their rounded noses were shaped a little like the front of an airliner. Every carriage had its own electric motors, following Shima's distributed power idea. The trains were designed to cruise at up to 210 km/h (130 mph), far faster than any regular train service in the world at that time. The line was about 515 km long, running from Tokyo to Shin-Ōsaka.

At first the railway ran a little cautiously while its brand-new track settled. The fastest service, called Hikari, meaning 'light', took 4 hours between Tokyo and Osaka. The stopping service, called Kodama, meaning 'echo', took 5 hours. By November 1965 the Hikari had been speeded up to 3 hours 10 minutes. The best express on the old line had needed more than six hours.

Passengers flocked to the new trains. About 100 million people had ridden the Tōkaidō Shinkansen by 1967, less than three years after it opened. By 2012 it had carried about 5.3 billion passengers, roughly three people for every four alive on the whole planet at that time. Daily ridership grew from about 61,000 in 1964 to more than 450,000 by 2016.

The original 0 Series trains served for 35 years before the last ones left the Tōkaidō line in 1999. Today the line's trains run at up to 285 km/h, and at the busiest times as many as 17 trains an hour leave Tokyo for the west. Japan kept extending its Shinkansen network north and south, to Hokkaido, Kyushu and the coast of the Sea of Japan, so that it now stretches roughly 3,000 km.

sections.heading: The Secrets of Speed
paragraphs: You might think that to make a train go faster, you just need a bigger engine. In fact, high-speed rail is a whole system, and every part had to be rethought.

First, the track. The Shinkansen runs on its own dedicated lines, separate from slow local and freight trains. It uses standard gauge, 1,435 mm, the same gauge that George Stephenson chose for his railways, rather than Japan's usual narrow gauge. The curves are very wide and gentle, because a train taking a sharp curve at high speed would push outward with huge force, uncomfortable for passengers and hard on the rails. There are no level crossings where roads cross the line; every road passes over or under it on a bridge. Much of the line runs on viaducts and embankments, with long tunnels through hills, so the track stays as straight and level as possible.

Second, the power. A train cruising at 200 km/h or more needs a great deal of energy, far more than it could carry in a fuel tank without becoming much heavier. So high-speed trains are electric. A high-voltage overhead wire, called the catenary, runs above the track, and pantographs on the roof press gently against it to collect electricity. That electricity drives traction motors spread along the train.

Third, the shape. At high speed, the biggest enemy is the air. Air resistance increases with the square of the speed: go twice as fast and the air pushes back about four times as hard. So bullet trains have smooth sides and streamlined noses. In Japan the nose has another job. When a fast train bursts into a narrow tunnel, it squeezes the air in front of it like a piston in a syringe, sending a pressure wave racing ahead. When that wave reaches the far end, it can burst out with a loud boom, a problem called 'tunnel boom'. That is one reason newer Shinkansen trains have very long, carefully sculpted noses, some of them more than 15 metres long, which ease into the tunnel gradually.

Fourth, the signals. Ordinary trains rely on signals beside the track. But at over 200 km/h, a driver would have only a split second to see a signal, and it would take several kilometres to stop. So the Shinkansen showed signal information inside the driver's cab, on the dashboard. This is called cab signalling. Even more important was automatic train control, or ATC. Electrical signals sent through the rails tell the train the maximum safe speed for each section of track. If the driver goes too fast, the ATC system applies the brakes automatically.

Finally, there is the people side: careful timetables, strict maintenance and constant inspection. Overnight, when no passenger trains run, special inspection trains and maintenance crews check the track and wires so that everything is perfect for the morning. In Japan the yellow track-inspection train is nicknamed Doctor Yellow, and spotting it is said by fans to bring good luck.

sections.heading: Safe, Punctual and Earthquake-Ready
paragraphs: Speed is impressive, but what has made the Shinkansen truly famous is how safe and reliable it is. In more than 60 years, carrying over 10 billion passengers, the Shinkansen has had no passenger deaths caused by its trains derailing or colliding in normal service. That is an astonishing record for any form of transport, let alone one that runs at nearly 300 km/h through one of the most earthquake-prone countries on Earth.

That does not mean nothing has ever gone wrong, and it is important to be accurate. On 23 October 2004 a powerful earthquake struck the Chūetsu region of Niigata Prefecture. A Jōetsu Shinkansen train called Toki 325 was travelling at speed near Nagaoka when the shaking hit, and eight of its ten cars came off the rails. Amazingly, none of the 154 passengers was killed or injured. Afterwards, engineers fitted new anti-derailment guides to the tracks to help keep wheels close to the rails even if a train is knocked sideways. In 2013 another train on the Akita Shinkansen line derailed in a blizzard, again with no injuries to passengers. Sadly, there have been a few deaths and injuries in other ways, such as a passenger who was caught in a closing door and dragged along a platform, which is why platform staff now watch the doors carefully.

How do you protect a train from earthquakes? Japan built a network of seismometers, instruments that detect ground shaking, along its lines and coasts. Earthquakes send out different kinds of waves. The first, faster waves are usually gentle; the slower waves that follow cause most of the damage. Since 1992 a warning system known as UrEDAS has been able to sense the first waves and automatically cut power to trains and apply their brakes, often seconds before the strongest shaking arrives. Seconds matter: a train braking early is travelling much more slowly when the ground starts to sway. Newer trains have also been made lighter and given stronger brakes so that they stop sooner.

Then there is punctuality, meaning being on time. On the Tōkaidō Shinkansen, the average delay per train is measured in seconds rather than minutes. JR Central, the company that runs the line, reported an average delay of only about 12 seconds per train in the 2019 financial year, even counting delays caused by storms and earthquakes. Train crews and station staff work to a precise timetable, and cleaning teams can tidy an entire train in just a few minutes while it waits at the terminus.

Winter weather is another enemy. Near Maibara, where snow often falls on the Tōkaidō line, sprinklers spray water onto the tracks to stop snow from piling up and freezing onto trains. On the snowy Jōetsu line in the mountains, even stronger sprinklers and special concrete slab track help trains keep running through snow two or three metres deep.

sections.heading: Europe Joins the Race
paragraphs: Japan's success made the rest of the world sit up. France was next. French engineers at first built an experimental train powered by gas turbines, a type of engine similar to those on jet aircraft. This prototype, TGV 001, reached 318 km/h in December 1972. But in 1973 the world was hit by an oil crisis, when the price of oil soared. Fuel-hungry gas turbines suddenly looked like a bad bet, and France had plenty of electricity from its power stations. So the production trains were made electric.

TGV stands for Train à Grande Vitesse, French for 'high-speed train'. Before opening, a test train reached 380 km/h on 26 February 1981, a new world record. Then, on 27 September 1981, the first TGVs began carrying the public on a new high-speed line between Paris and Lyon. TGV carriages share their wheel sets: instead of each coach having two sets of wheels of its own, the ends of neighbouring coaches rest on the same bogie. This articulated design makes the train lighter and helps it stay upright and in line even if it derails, one reason TGVs have not had a passenger death in an accident on their high-speed lines in normal service for more than four decades. On 28 November 2003 the TGV network carried its billionth passenger.

The French loved breaking records. In 1990 a TGV reached 515.3 km/h. Then, on 3 April 2007, a specially modified train nicknamed V150 roared along the new LGV Est line east of Paris. It had extra-large wheels, extra power, and the voltage in the overhead wire was raised from the usual 25,000 volts to 31,000 volts. The wire was also pulled tighter, so that the pantograph would not set up waves in it at such tremendous speed. The train reached 574.8 km/h (357 mph). That is still the world speed record for a train running on ordinary steel wheels and rails. At that speed you could travel from London to Paris in well under an hour.

Germany followed with its InterCityExpress, or ICE. An experimental version set a world record of 406.9 km/h on 1 May 1988, and regular ICE services began on 2 June 1991, linking Hamburg with Frankfurt and Munich. Germany's high-speed story also includes a tragedy. On 3 June 1998 an ICE train crashed near the village of Eschede after a tiny fatigue crack caused the steel tyre of one of its wheels to break apart. The train derailed at a switch and hit a road bridge, and 101 people died. Investigators found that the wheel design had not been properly tested for repeated stress. Germany quickly replaced those wheels with solid one-piece wheels and changed its safety rules, lessons that helped make high-speed rail safer worldwide.

High-speed trains changed the way people chose to travel. When the AVE first opened, its non-stop trains covered the Madrid to Seville route in 2 hours 45 minutes, and by 1994, running at up to 300 km/h, the fastest trains took about 2 hours 20 minutes. Journeys like that are short enough that, once you count the time spent getting to an airport, checking in and waiting at the gate, the train often wins. On routes such as Paris to Lyon and Madrid to Seville, many travellers who once flew switched to the train, and airlines cut their flights.

Spain opened its first high-speed line, called AVE, in April 1992, just in time for the world's fair Expo 92 in Seville. The line ran about 472 km from Madrid to Seville. Spain's older railways used a broad 'Iberian' gauge, wider than most of Europe, but the new line was built to standard gauge so that it could one day connect to the rest of Europe. Today Spain has one of the largest high-speed networks in the world, and other countries, including Italy, Belgium, the Netherlands, South Korea, Taiwan and Turkey, have joined the high-speed club too.

sections.heading: Under the Sea and Through the Alps
paragraphs: Fast trains need straight, level tracks, and sometimes the only way to get them is to go underground. The late 20th century became an age of record-breaking railway tunnels.

Japan led again. Its main island, Honshu, is separated from the northern island of Hokkaido by the stormy Tsugaru Strait. In 1954 a typhoon sank the ferry Tōya Maru in the strait, and about 1,430 people died. The disaster convinced the government that a fixed link was needed. Work on the Seikan Tunnel began in 1971. Workers battled flooding and crumbling rock, and 34 of them died during construction. When the tunnel opened in March 1988, it was 53.85 km long, with about 23.3 km running beneath the seabed. Its track lies around 240 metres below sea level. Since 2016 Shinkansen trains have run through it on the way to Hokkaido.

Between Britain and France, people had dreamed of a tunnel under the English Channel since Napoleon's time. Finally, in the late 1980s, eleven giant tunnel boring machines started chewing through a layer of soft rock called chalk marl, which is easy to dig yet fairly waterproof. At the peak of construction about 15,000 people worked on the project. On 1 December 1990 British and French workers broke through and shook hands deep beneath the sea. The Channel Tunnel actually consists of three tunnels: two for trains and a smaller service tunnel between them for maintenance and emergencies. It is about 50.5 km long, and its 37.9 km undersea section is the longest of any tunnel in the world, reaching about 75 metres below sea level.

Queen Elizabeth II and French President François Mitterrand opened the tunnel on 6 May 1994. In November 1994 Eurostar passenger trains began running through it, linking London with Paris and Brussels. It cost far more than planned, about 80 percent over budget, but it changed travel between Britain and mainland Europe for good.

Then came the mountains. Switzerland sits in the middle of the Alps, and lorries carrying goods between northern and southern Europe were clogging its mountain roads. In 1992 Swiss voters approved a plan to build new flat railway routes through the Alps. The centrepiece was the Gotthard Base Tunnel. Instead of climbing up the mountains and spiralling down the other side, like the old Gotthard railway of 1882, trains would pass right through the base of the mountains.

Digging began in 1999. In places the tunnel lies about 2,450 metres beneath the mountain peaks above, and the rock was so hot that the tunnels had to be cooled for workers. The eastern tube broke through on 15 October 2010. Sadly, nine workers died during construction. The tunnel was opened on 1 June 2016 and began regular service that December. At about 57 km long, it is the longest railway tunnel in the world, and its highest point is only about 549 metres above sea level, making it the first flat route through the Alps. Passenger trains can pass through at up to 200 km/h.

sections.heading: China's Giant Leap
paragraphs: The most dramatic high-speed story of all began in 2008. On 1 August that year, a week before the Beijing Olympics opened, China opened a high-speed line between Beijing and the port city of Tianjin. It offered the first commercial train service in the world scheduled to run at 350 km/h (217 mph). Passengers loved it: the short Beijing to Tianjin line alone carried more than 41 million riders in its first two years.

China had studied the world's best high-speed trains and arranged to build versions of them at home, using designs from Japan's Kawasaki, Germany's Siemens, France's Alstom and Canada's Bombardier. Chinese engineers soon developed their own models. In June 2011 a line opened between Beijing and Shanghai, China's two biggest cities.

The fast growth brought a hard lesson. On 23 July 2011 two high-speed trains collided on a viaduct near the city of Wenzhou after signalling failures during a thunderstorm. Officially, 40 people died. The government paused approvals of new lines and reduced top speeds on many routes while safety was reviewed. From 2017 new Chinese-designed trains called Fuxing, meaning 'rejuvenation', brought 350 km/h running back to several major lines.

After that, construction went on at an astonishing pace. By 2020 China had about 37,900 km of high-speed railway, and by the early 2020s it had more than 40,000 km, more than the rest of the world combined. The network has since passed about 50,000 km, roughly two-thirds of all the high-speed track on Earth. Gleaming stations as big as airports have been built in city after city, and on busy holidays such as the Lunar New Year, hundreds of millions of journeys are made on China's railways.

From Japan's first bullet train in 1964 to China's vast network today, high-speed rail has shown that trains are not old-fashioned at all. Yet even the fastest steel wheel has a limit. At extreme speeds, wheels and rails wear quickly, the pantograph struggles to stay in contact with the wire, and the train needs huge power just to push the air aside. So engineers have asked a daring question: if wheels have a speed limit, what if a train had no wheels touching the track at all?

deepDive: High-speed rail is usually defined as passenger service at about 250 km/h or more on newly built lines, or about 200 km/h on upgraded older lines. Why not simply run trains faster on old tracks? The physics of curves explains much of it. A train on a curve needs a sideways (centripetal) force equal to its mass times speed squared divided by the curve's radius, so doubling speed needs a curve four times as wide to keep the same comfort and the same force on the rails. Tilting the track (cant) helps, but only up to a limit, because slow trains on the same track would then lean inwards uncomfortably. That is a strong argument for dedicated passenger-only lines like the Shinkansen. Air resistance is the other wall: drag grows roughly with the square of speed, so the power needed to overcome it grows roughly with the cube. Going from 300 to 360 km/h needs about 70 percent more power just for the air. The 2007 V150 record at 574.8 km/h needed extra-large wheels, boosted voltage and specially tensioned catenary, conditions no commercial service could sustain cheaply, which is why most high-speed trains cruise at 300 to 350 km/h. Debates continue about cost and value. Supporters point to big cuts in short-haul flights where fast trains compete: when a train journey takes under about three to four hours, many travellers switch from planes, as happened between Madrid and Seville and between Paris and Lyon. Critics point to huge construction costs and debts, cost overruns from the Tōkaidō line to the Channel Tunnel and Britain's HS2, and some lightly used lines. China's boom has been especially debated: its national railway operator carries large debts, and some economists question whether every line will repay its cost, while others argue that faster connections between cities bring wider economic and environmental benefits that ticket sales alone do not capture. Safety lessons have shaped the whole field: the Eschede disaster changed wheel design and testing, and the Wenzhou collision led China to review signalling. Historians also note that the Shinkansen's success came from an integrated system, combining track, trains, signalling, maintenance and timetables, rather than from any single invention.
funFact: The nickname 'bullet train' is older than the Shinkansen itself: it translates dangan ressha, a name Japanese newspapers gave to a planned fast railway back in 1939.
